changes.before: If both declared column classes become numeric, how is ID 001 printed?
changes.after: A table ID may look like a number even when its leading zeros matter.

before: read.csv reads delimited text into a data frame. Here text supplies a tiny literal CSV rather than an external path. colClasses declares the ID as character and minutes as numeric, so leading zeros in an identifier are not mistaken for numeric magnitude.

An imported column still needs its meaning, missing-value policy and valid range checked. stringsAsFactors = FALSE makes the intended text treatment explicit. Never assume a plausible inferred type proves that units, IDs or measurements were interpreted correctly.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
data <- read.csv(text = "id,minutes\n001,15\n", colClasses = c("character", "numeric"),
                 stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
cat(data$id, "\n", sep = "")
cat(data$minutes, "\n", sep = "")

```

Expected output or behavior: 001
15. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Keep the ID as text and read minutes as a number.

Follow the labeled parts of this example.
```r
data <- read.csv(text = "id,minutes\n001,15\n", colClasses = c("character", "numeric"),
                 stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
cat(data$id, "\n", sep = "")
cat(data$minutes, "\n", sep = "")
```
The output is `001`, then `15`. The ID keeps both leading zeros. Fifteen remains a numeric minute count.
Import the ID column as a number instead.

before.question: If both declared column classes become numeric, how is ID 001 printed?
choices: 001 because CSV preserves every field as text.

before.explanation: The numeric conversion retains magnitude but not leading-zero formatting; an ID should have remained character.

after.question: If ID 001 is read as numeric, how does it print?
after.explanation: The number is one. Its original leading zeros are not stored.
